name: Russell's Teapot
statement: The burden of proof for an unfalsifiable claim lies with whoever asserts it.
meaning: If you assert that something exists which, by design, can never be checked or refuted, it is on you to give reasons to believe it. Others are not obliged to disprove it, and their inability to do so lends the claim no credibility.
mechanism: A positive existence claim carries the obligation of evidence; shifting that onto the sceptic, 'prove it doesn't exist', is an illegitimate reversal of the burden of proof. And when a claim is built so that no possible observation could contradict it (a teapot 'too small to be revealed by our most powerful telescopes'), its immunity from refutation is a defect, not a strength: it makes the claim epistemically empty rather than probable.

examples.text: Russell aimed the analogy at the demand that atheists disprove God: the one making the positive, unfalsifiable claim bears the burden, and its unfalsifiability is no reason to accept it. It remains a staple of philosophy-of-religion debate.
Bobby Henderson's 2005 satirical deity makes the same point: an arbitrary, unfalsifiable entity is exactly as 'provable' as any other, so unfalsifiability cannot be what makes a claim believable.
Carl Sagan's invisible, heatless, incorporeal dragon (every test for it pre-empted by an excuse) shows that a claim insulated from all possible disproof is indistinguishable from no claim at all.

variants.name: Hitchens's razor
variants.text: The dismissal that follows from the same logic: what can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.

variants.name: The Sagan standard
variants.text: Its close relative on the demand side: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and an unfalsifiable one supplies none.

variants.name: The invisible pink unicorn
variants.text: Another parody entity used, like the teapot, to expose that unfalsifiability confers no support on a claim.

whyItMatters: It is the sharpest short statement of where the burden of proof sits, and of why 'you can't prove me wrong' is not an argument. It gives a name to the move of demanding disproof of the undisprovable, and shows why that move fails.

working.lead: Keep the burden on the claimant
working.text: the one asserting that something exists owes the evidence; do not accept a demand that you disprove it instead.

working.lead: Treat unfalsifiability as a red flag
working.text: a claim engineered so nothing could ever count against it has bought its safety at the price of saying anything at all.
that no one has refuted a claim is not evidence for it: countless unfalsifiable claims share that status.

limits: It is a rhetorical analogy about where the burden of proof lies, not a disproof of God or anything else. It shows a demand is illegitimate, not that a claim is false. Critics press disanalogy objections: Brian Garvey argues theism-versus-atheism is a clash of whole worldviews rather than a dispute over one object, and Alvin Plantinga notes there is positive evidence against an orbiting teapot (no one launched one) that has no clean parallel for other claims. The teapot sharpens the burden-of-proof intuition; it does not settle the underlying questions.
misreadings: It is not an argument that God, or anything else, does not exist — Russell was explicit that the teapot cannot be disproved either. The point is narrower: unfalsifiability is not a reason to believe, and the burden lies with the one who asserts.
origin: Bertrand Russell devised the celestial-teapot analogy in an article, 'Is There a God?', commissioned by Illustrated magazine in 1952 but never published in his lifetime. He imagined a china teapot orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small for any telescope to reveal — unfalsifiable, yet no one should believe in it on that basis; if such a teapot were affirmed in ancient books and taught to children, he added, doubting it would be treated as eccentric.

sources.text: Russell, B. (1952). "Is There a God?" — commissioned by Illustrated; first published posthumously in his Collected Papers, vol. 11.
